headline: Facebook found liable for deceiving users in Cambridge Analytica case
summary: A New Mexico jury found Facebook liable for deceiving users about privacy protections in the Cambridge Analytica data breach. The state is seeking a maximum penalty of $5,000 per violation.
details: A New Mexico jury has found Facebook liable for deceiving users regarding privacy protections on its social media platform. This verdict stems from the Cambridge Analytica data breach, with state attorneys seeking a maximum penalty of $5,000 per violation.

The two-week trial centered on accusations that Facebook misled users about a third-party personality quiz. This quiz harvested data from approximately 87 million profiles and sold it to Cambridge Analytica, a political consulting firm, for targeted ads.

Jurors sided with prosecutors, determining that Facebook's failure to protect user data impacted New Mexico's entire population of over 2 million people. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez hailed the verdict as "historic."
Furthermore, the jury found Facebook liable for over 2 million violations for misleading the public about investigations into data brokers following the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

Lawyers for Facebook argued the state's evidence was outdated. A Meta spokesperson stated the company disagrees with the verdict and will continue to defend against efforts to "distort our records," emphasizing First Amendment rights.

New Mexico was the only state to pursue this specific case, as Meta had previously agreed to an $18 billion multistate settlement. That settlement included an agreement to release Meta from future liability related to the Cambridge Analytica privacy breach.

Earlier this year, New Mexico also secured $942 million in judgments from Meta in a separate trial concerning child safety issues. The court ordered Meta to implement new safeguards, including age-verification technology and time limits on its platforms.

headline_marked: [[Meta showcases new audio-only smart glasses]] and $150 hearing-aid specs at Connect
headline: Meta showcases new audio-only smart glasses and $150 hearing-aid specs at Connect
summary: Meta's latest Connect event heavily featured its smart glasses line, including new camera-free models addressing privacy concerns and specialized glasses for the hearing impaired at a significantly lower price point.
details: Meta Connect 2023 clearly demonstrated the company's strong commitment to its smart glasses initiative. The devices were ubiquitous at the annual event, worn by both staff and influencers, and featured prominently in most product demonstrations.

Among the notable products demoed were new, unreleased audio-only smart glasses, designed to mitigate privacy concerns. This follows previous accusations regarding camera-equipped models being used for surveillance.

These new glasses feature six microphones but no camera, eliminating native recording capabilities. They are also significantly lighter and more comfortable than previous models, focusing on entertainment and communication.

The audio-only glasses will integrate with Muse, Meta's personal agentic system, allowing users to verbally give commands. This integration, not yet public, aims to personalize the agent with digital avatars.

While interacting with Muse requires direct communication and avoids simultaneous conversations, its potential for hands-free task management is clear. Users could ask Muse to send emails, recite to-do lists, or answer questions like a mobile ChatGPT.
Another significant demo was a second pair of audio-only glasses specifically for the hearing impaired. These glasses, developed over five years, aim to address hearing loss, which affects millions.

Crucially, these hearing-impaired glasses are projected to sell for $150, a stark contrast to many hearing aids that can cost up to $1,600. They amplify voices, with users able to switch between focused and omnidirectional sound pickup.

Mark Zuckerberg views smart glasses as the future, and Meta is casting a wide net to make them stylish, functional, and useful. The company hopes to succeed where others have struggled in making smart glasses a mainstream device.
